q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

items.q: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the student's claim?
items.p: In the poem "Harbor at Dusk," the speaker describes a small fishing harbor at the end of a long working day. A student claims that the poem conveys a feeling of quiet rest after a day of hard effort.
c: "The nets hang folded, and the tired boats / lean softly on the slow and settling tide."
"Gulls shriek and dive above the churning wake."
"The engines roar before the break of day."
"Ropes snap taut against the rising wind."
w: Shrieking gulls and churning water suggest noise and motion, not rest.
This describes the start of the day and loud engines.
Snapping ropes and rising wind suggest tension, not rest.
items.e: Folded nets, "tired boats," and a "settling tide" together suggest calm after work.

items.p:
| Month | Tickets sold |
| January | 1,200 |
| February | 1,450 |
| March | 1,900 |

The manager of the Westfield Theater claims that ticket sales grew each month from January through March.
c: Sales rose from 1,200 tickets in January to 1,450 in February and 1,900 in March.
The theater sold 1,450 tickets in February.
The theater sold fewer tickets in March than in January.
The theater sold 1,200 tickets in January.
w: One month's total can't show growth from month to month.
This is false; March sales were higher.
One month's total can't show growth from month to month.
items.e: Only this choice shows sales rising in each step: 1,200 → 1,450 → 1,900.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Abara's argument?
items.p: Historian Ruth Abara argues that the Valley Courier, a newspaper published in the 1890s, strongly supported the construction of a new railroad through its county. She bases her argument on the paper's surviving issues.
c: The Courier printed many editorials praising the railroad's expected benefits.
The Courier was founded in 1871.
The railroad was completed in 1896.
Rival newspapers opposed the railroad.
w: The founding date says nothing about the paper's position.
The completion date says nothing about the paper's position.
Other papers' views don't show the Courier's view.
items.e: Editorials praising the railroad would directly show the Courier's support.

items.p:
| Year | Herons counted |
| 2019 | 42 |
| 2020 | 51 |
| 2021 | 63 |
| 2022 | 70 |

Volunteers at Lake Orin count herons each spring. A volunteer claims that the number of herons counted at the lake increased every year from 2019 to 2022.
c: The count rose every year, from 42 in 2019 to 70 in 2022.
Volunteers counted 51 herons in 2020.
The count fell between 2021 and 2022.
More herons were counted in 2019 than in 2022.
w: One year's count can't show a yearly increase.
This is false: the count rose from 63 to 70.
This is false: 42 is less than 70.
items.e: The counts rise in each year shown: 42, 51, 63, 70.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
items.p: Researchers studying the amber leaf beetle, an insect that damages fruit trees, hypothesize that the beetle is strongly attracted to the color yellow. If so, farmers could use yellow traps to protect their orchards.
c: Traps painted yellow caught far more beetles than identical traps painted other colors.
The beetles are found in orchards in many countries.
Yellow flowers bloom earlier in spring than other flowers.
Traps of every color caught similar numbers of beetles.
w: Where the beetles live says nothing about color preference.
This concerns flowers, not the beetles' behavior.
This would weaken the hypothesis.
items.e: If yellow traps catch far more beetles than otherwise identical traps, the beetles are drawn to yellow.

items.p:
| Exhibit | Average daily visitors |
| Fossils | 340 |
| Space | 510 |
| Textiles | 190 |

A museum guide claims that the space exhibit was the most popular of the three exhibits shown.
c: The space exhibit averaged 510 visitors a day, more than the fossil (340) and textile (190) exhibits.
The fossil exhibit averaged 340 visitors a day.
The textile exhibit had the fewest visitors.
The fossil and textile exhibits together averaged 530 visitors a day.
w: This gives one exhibit's figure without comparing it to the space exhibit.
This is true but doesn't show that the space exhibit was most popular.
Combining two exhibits doesn't compare each one to the space exhibit.
items.e: Only this choice compares the space exhibit's figure with both of the others.

items.q: Which quotation from the story most effectively illustrates the student's claim?
items.p: In a short story, the narrator, a young violinist, waits backstage before her first solo performance. A student claims that the narrator feels nervous in the moments before she walks onstage.
c: "My hands would not stop shaking as I tuned the violin for the third time."
"The hall was painted a pale, cheerful blue."
"My teacher had chosen the piece months earlier."
"Afterward, we all went out for a late dinner."
w: The hall's color doesn't show how the narrator feels.
This gives background, not a feeling.
This happens after the performance.
items.e: Shaking hands and retuning the violin again and again show nervousness.

items.p:
| Transportation | Share of respondents |
| Bus | 34% |
| Train | 22% |
| Bicycle | 9% |
| Car | 35% |

A city report claims that more survey respondents use public transit, meaning buses and trains combined, than use cars.
c: Buses (34%) and trains (22%) together account for 56% of respondents, compared with 35% for cars.
Cars are used by 35% of respondents, more than buses alone (34%).
Bicycles are used by 9% of respondents.
Trains are used by 22% of respondents, fewer than cars.
w: This compares cars with buses alone, which seems to undercut the claim.
Bicycles are not part of the claim.
This compares trains alone with cars and doesn't combine transit.
items.e: The claim is about buses and trains combined, and 34% + 22% = 56% is greater than 35%.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the scientists' claim?
items.p: Algae blooms have become common in Lake Merin. Some scientists claim that the blooms are caused mainly by fertilizer washing into the lake from nearby farms, rather than by rising water temperatures.
c: Blooms were just as frequent in years when nearby farms used little fertilizer as in years when they used a lot.
Farms near the lake have used fertilizer for decades.
Blooms are most common in the summer months.
The amount of fertilizer washing into the lake has increased in recent years.
w: This is consistent with the claim.
Summer has both more runoff and warmer water, so this doesn't separate the causes.
This, if anything, supports the claim.
items.e: If blooms don't change when fertilizer use changes, fertilizer is unlikely to be the main cause.

items.p:
| Hours of sleep | Average reaction time (milliseconds) |
| 5 | 410 |
| 6 | 380 |
| 7 | 350 |
| 8 | 330 |

Researchers claim that participants who slept more the night before a test tended to react faster.
c: Average reaction time fell from 410 milliseconds for 5 hours of sleep to 330 milliseconds for 8 hours.
Participants who slept 6 hours averaged 380 milliseconds.
Reaction times rose as hours of sleep increased.
Participants who slept 7 hours had an average reaction time of 350 milliseconds.
w: One data point can't show a trend.
This is false; reaction times fell.
One data point can't show a trend.
items.e: Lower reaction times mean faster reactions, and times fall steadily as sleep increases.

items.q: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the critic's claim?
items.p: Literary critic Omar Sayed claims that in the novel The Glass Orchard, the main character's growing confidence is shown mainly through how she speaks to her employer over the course of a year.
c: "At first she answered only 'Yes, sir'; by winter she was the one asking the questions."
"The orchard stretched for miles beyond the house."
"Her employer owned three farms in the valley."
"She had always loved the smell of ripe apples."
w: This describes the setting, not her speech.
This describes the employer's property.
This describes a preference, not growing confidence.
items.e: The shift from "Yes, sir" to asking questions shows her confidence growing in how she speaks to her employer.

items.p:
| Month | Ashford rainfall (mm) | Bellvue rainfall (mm) |
| April | 80 | 65 |
| May | 95 | 70 |
| June | 60 | 55 |

A geography student claims that Ashford received more rain than Bellvue in every month shown.
c: In each month, Ashford's rainfall was higher: 80 vs. 65 mm in April, 95 vs. 70 in May, and 60 vs. 55 in June.
Ashford received 95 mm of rain in May.
Bellvue received less rain in June than in May.
Both cities received the least rain in June.
w: One month doesn't show every month.
This compares Bellvue with itself.
This doesn't compare the two cities.
items.e: The claim is about every month, so the support must compare both cities in each month.

items.p:
| Soil temperature | Species A germination | Species B germination |
| 10°C | 20% | 45% |
| 20°C | 65% | 50% |
| 30°C | 80% | 40% |

A botanist hypothesizes that warmer soil benefits the germination of species A more than it benefits species B.
c: From 10°C to 30°C, species A's germination rose from 20% to 80%, while species B's fell from 45% to 40%.
At 10°C, species B germinated at a higher rate than species A.
At 20°C, species A germinated at 65% and species B at 50%.
Species B germinated at 40% at 30°C.
w: This is one temperature and doesn't show the effect of warming.
This is one temperature and doesn't show change.
This gives one value for one species.
items.e: The hypothesis concerns how each species responds to warming, which requires comparing their changes from cool to warm soil.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitford's argument?
items.p: After the city of Danvers added bike lanes to several commercial streets, some shop owners feared that losing parking spaces would hurt their sales. Economist Dana Whitford argues that the bike lanes did not reduce sales at nearby shops.
c: Sales at shops on streets with new bike lanes changed by about the same amount as sales at similar shops on streets without them.
Many shop owners opposed the bike lanes before construction.
The number of cyclists using the lanes rose steadily after they opened.
Sales at shops on streets with bike lanes rose during the holiday season.
w: Owners' fears are not evidence about sales.
Lane use doesn't show what happened to sales.
Without a comparison, a holiday rise could happen anywhere.
items.e: Comparing similar shops with and without bike lanes isolates the lanes' effect. Similar changes suggest no harm.

items.p:
| Age group | Read a print newspaper weekly |
| 18–29 | 12% |
| 30–49 | 21% |
| 50–64 | 38% |
| 65 and older | 55% |

A media researcher claims that weekly print newspaper reading becomes more common with each older age group.
c: The share rises with each age group, from 12% of adults aged 18–29 to 55% of those 65 and older.
38% of adults aged 50–64 read a print newspaper weekly.
Fewer than a quarter of adults aged 30–49 read a print newspaper weekly.
Adults aged 18–29 read print newspapers more often than adults aged 30–49.
w: One group can't show a pattern across groups.
This is true but doesn't compare the groups.
This is false: 12% is less than 21%.
items.e: The claim is about a steady rise across all groups, and 12%, 21%, 38%, and 55% show exactly that.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologists' hypothesis?
items.p: A species of small wasp lays its eggs inside caterpillars. Biologists hypothesize that the wasps locate host caterpillars mainly by scent rather than by sight.
c: Wasps found caterpillars hidden inside sealed, opaque mesh bags as quickly as they found caterpillars left in plain view.
Wasps found visible caterpillars faster than hidden ones.
The wasps are active only during daylight hours.
Caterpillars release a distinctive scent when they chew leaves.
w: This suggests sight matters, which weakens the hypothesis.
Daytime activity, if anything, hints that sight matters.
This shows a scent exists, not that wasps use it.
items.e: If hiding the caterpillars from view doesn't slow the wasps, they must be using something other than sight, such as scent.

items.p:
| City | Average commute 2010 (minutes) | Average commute 2020 (minutes) |
| Arden | 24 | 27 |
| Bellmont | 31 | 29 |
| Cresby | 19 | 26 |

An urban planner claims that, of the three cities, Cresby saw the largest increase in average commute time between 2010 and 2020.
c: Cresby's average commute rose by 7 minutes, more than Arden's 3-minute rise, while Bellmont's fell.
Bellmont had the longest average commute in both years.
Arden's average commute rose from 24 to 27 minutes.
Cresby had the shortest average commute in 2010.
w: This is true but concerns length, not change.
This describes only Arden.
This is true but concerns one year, not change.
items.e: The claim compares increases, and Cresby rose 7 minutes, Arden 3, and Bellmont fell 2.

items.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's claim?
items.p: In the 1880s, the city of Haverly built several large public bathhouses. Historian Paulo Brandt claims that the city built the bathhouses mainly to improve public health rather than to provide places of leisure.
c: City council records describe the bathhouses' purpose as reducing the spread of disease in crowded districts.
The bathhouses included gardens and a café.
Many residents visited the bathhouses on weekends.
The bathhouses were among the largest buildings in the city.
w: Leisure features, if anything, weaken the claim.
Weekend visits suggest leisure use and don't show the city's purpose.
Size doesn't indicate purpose.
items.e: Records stating the bathhouses' purpose as disease prevention directly support a public-health motive.
